stem: Shoulder weakness after neck pain. Sensory conductions normal.
why: Rhomboid and paraspinals are abnormal. The dorsal scapular nerve leaves the C5 root before the upper trunk forms, and paraspinals come off the dorsal ramus, so the lesion is at the root.

stem: Shoulder and elbow-flexion weakness after a fall onto the shoulder. Lateral antebrachial cutaneous SNAP is low.
why: C5–6 muscles from several nerves are involved, but rhomboid, serratus and paraspinals (all supplied before the trunk) are spared, and a SNAP is abnormal. That places the lesion distal to the roots: upper trunk.

options: Radial neuropathy at the spiral groove
stem: Neck pain radiating to the middle finger, weak elbow extension. Sensory conductions normal.
why: Triceps (radial) plus FCR and pronator teres (median) share C7 but come from different nerves, and paraspinals are abnormal. In Levin's surgical series, triceps and FCR were the most reliable C7 muscles.

options: Radial neuropathy at the spiral groove
stem: Weak shoulder abduction, elbow extension and wrist extension after a shoulder dislocation. Radial SNAP low.
why: Axillary (deltoid), thoracodorsal (latissimus) and radial muscles are all involved. Those three nerves meet only at the posterior cord. Biceps and FCR are normal, so this isn't a trunk lesion.

answer: Radial neuropathy at the spiral groove
options: Radial neuropathy at the spiral groove
stem: Woke with a wrist drop after sleeping on the arm. Superficial radial SNAP low.
why: Brachioradialis is abnormal, so the lesion is above the elbow. Triceps is spared because its branches leave the radial nerve before the spiral groove.

options: Radial neuropathy at the spiral groove
stem: Finger drop with preserved wrist extension (wrist deviates radially). Superficial radial SNAP normal.
why: Brachioradialis and ECRL branch off above the PIN, so they're spared and the wrist pulls radially. The normal superficial radial SNAP fits a pure motor branch.

stem: Hand weakness with numbness of the little finger. Ulnar and medial antebrachial SNAPs normal.
why: EIP is a C8 muscle on the radial nerve, so its involvement rules out ulnar neuropathy. Normal SNAPs (the lesion is proximal to the dorsal root ganglion) plus abnormal paraspinals point to the root.

stem: Numb ring and little fingers, weak grip. Ulnar SNAP low; ulnar motor slowing across the elbow.
why: FDP III–IV is involved, so the lesion is above the forearm branches. EIP and APB (C8 on other nerves) are normal, so it isn't the root or the lower trunk. FCU is often spared even in elbow lesions, so don't rely on it.

stem: Painless wasting of the first dorsal interosseous in a cyclist. No sensory symptoms; ulnar SNAP normal.
why: Only muscles of the deep branch beyond the hypothenar branches are affected. Hypothenar muscles, palmaris brevis (superficial branch) and the sensory SNAP are spared.

stem: Thenar wasting more than hypothenar in a young woman with a cervical rib. Medial antebrachial cutaneous SNAP low, ulnar SNAP low.
why: C8–T1 muscles across median, ulnar and radial nerves are involved, with low SNAPs and normal paraspinals: a lesion distal to the root. The thenar-predominant pattern is the classic neurogenic TOS hand.

stem: Can't make an 'OK' sign. No numbness; median SNAPs normal.
why: Only the AIN's three muscles are involved. APB (median, below the AIN branch) and pronator teres/FCR (above it) are normal, and the AIN has no cutaneous branch.

stem: Night-time numbness of the thumb to ring finger. Median sensory latency prolonged.
why: Only the thenar muscle beyond the carpal tunnel is involved. FPL and pronator teres (median, proximal) and FDI (C8, ulnar) are normal.

answer: Suprascapular neuropathy at the spinoglenoid notch
options: Suprascapular neuropathy at the spinoglenoid notch
Suprascapular neuropathy at the suprascapular notch
stem: Volleyball player with painless external-rotation weakness. MRI shows a labral cyst.
why: Supraspinatus gets its branch before the spinoglenoid notch, so isolated infraspinatus involvement places the lesion there.

stem: Medial scapular winging after carrying a heavy backpack.
why: Isolated serratus involvement with medial winging. Trapezius (spinal accessory) palsy causes lateral winging; rhomboid involvement would suggest C5 or the dorsal scapular nerve.

options: Common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head
stem: Foot drop with back pain. Superficial peroneal SNAP normal.
why: Tibialis posterior (tibial) and gluteus medius (superior gluteal) share L5 with the peroneal muscles. Their involvement, plus paraspinals and a normal SNAP, places the lesion at the root.

answer: Common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head
options: Common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head
stem: Foot drop after weight loss and leg crossing. Superficial peroneal SNAP low; conduction block across the fibular head.
why: Deep and superficial peroneal muscles are involved, but the short head of biceps femoris (peroneal division above the knee) is normal, so the lesion is at or below the fibular head. Normal tibialis posterior rules out L5.

options: Common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head
stem: Foot drop after hip arthroplasty. Superficial peroneal and sural SNAPs low.
why: The short head of biceps femoris is abnormal, so the lesion is above the knee. Gluteal muscles and paraspinals are normal, so it's distal to the plexus: the sciatic nerve (peroneal fibres are often hit hardest).

stem: Posterior calf pain, absent ankle reflex. Sural SNAP normal.
why: Gluteus maximus (inferior gluteal) is involved along with tibial-nerve muscles, so the lesion is above the sciatic nerve. Paraspinals plus a normal sural SNAP put it at the S1 root.

answer: Femoral neuropathy below the inguinal ligament
options: Femoral neuropathy below the inguinal ligament
stem: Knee buckling after a cardiac catheterization via the groin. Saphenous SNAP low.
why: Iliacus is supplied inside the pelvis, so a normal iliacus places the femoral lesion below the inguinal ligament. Normal adductor longus (obturator) rules out the root and plexus.

options: Femoral neuropathy below the inguinal ligament
stem: Thigh weakness on anticoagulation; CT shows an iliacus hematoma. Saphenous SNAP low.
why: Iliacus involvement puts the lesion above the inguinal ligament. Normal adductor longus and paraspinals keep it on the femoral nerve rather than the root or plexus.

options: Femoral neuropathy below the inguinal ligament
stem: Anterior thigh pain and a reduced patellar reflex. Saphenous SNAP normal.
why: Femoral (vastus lateralis, iliacus) and obturator (adductor longus) muscles share L3–4. Paraspinals plus a normal SNAP put the lesion at the root.
